slides.title: What is Blockchain?
slides.definition: A blockchain is a distributed, decentralized digital ledger that permanently records transactions across a peer-to-peer network of computers. It is append-only, cryptographically secured, and requires consensus among participants before any new data is added.
keyPoints: Introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in the 2008 Bitcoin whitepaper — 'A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System'
Data is organized into 'blocks' — each block is cryptographically linked to the one before it, forming a 'chain'
No central authority owns or controls the ledger — all participants (nodes) hold an identical copy

Immutability: once a block is confirmed and buried under subsequent blocks, altering it requires re-doing the computational work for every block that follows — practically impossible on large networks
Trust is provided by mathematics and cryptography, not by banks, governments, or intermediaries
Three pillars: Decentralization (no single owner), Transparency (publicly auditable), Security (cryptographic proofs)

slides.title: Blocks & Chains — Deep Structure
leftItems: Version — protocol rules this block follows
Timestamp — Unix time when block was created
Previous Block Hash — SHA-256 of the prior block header (creates the chain link)
Merkle Root — root hash of all transactions in this block
Nonce — 32-bit number miners iterate to find valid hash
Difficulty Target — required number of leading zeros in hash
Transaction Counter — number of transactions included
Transaction List — full list of validated transactions
rightItems: Block 0 = Genesis Block (hardcoded, no predecessor hash)
Each new block stores the hash of its parent — breaking one link breaks every link after it
Changing a single transaction in Block 5 changes its hash, which invalidates Block 6's stored hash, cascading through every block to the present
Longest valid chain rule — nodes always accept the chain with most accumulated proof-of-work
Orphan blocks — two valid blocks found simultaneously; one is eventually discarded as the chain grows
Block time: Bitcoin ~10 min | Ethereum ~12 sec | Solana ~400 ms

slides.title: Merkle Trees — How Transactions Are Fingerprinted
slides.definition: A Merkle Tree is a binary tree of hashes where each leaf node is a hash of a transaction, and each parent node is the hash of its two children. The Merkle Root (stored in the block header) is a single 32-byte fingerprint of ALL transactions in the block.
keyPoints: Efficient verification: to prove a single transaction exists in a block, you only need O(log n) hashes — not all thousands of transactions
Tamper detection: changing any one transaction changes its leaf hash, which bubbles up and changes the Merkle Root — instantly detectable
SPV (Simplified Payment Verification): light-weight mobile wallets use Merkle proofs to verify transactions without downloading the full blockchain
Bitcoin uses double SHA-256 for Merkle nodes: Hash = SHA256(SHA256(data))
Ethereum uses a modified Patricia Merkle Trie — three tries per block: Transactions Trie, Receipts Trie, State Trie
Real-world analogy: think of the Merkle Root as a checksum for the entire contents of a block

slides.title: Decentralization & Node Types
slides.intro: The blockchain network is maintained by thousands of independently operated nodes worldwide. No single entity can shut it down — there is no central server, no CEO, no off switch.
bullets: Full Nodes — download and independently verify every block and every transaction ever made; enforce all consensus rules; most important for network integrity
Pruned Full Nodes — verify the full chain but discard old transaction data after verification to save disk space
Light Nodes (SPV) — download only block headers (~80 bytes each); rely on full nodes for transaction data; used in mobile wallets
Mining / Validator Nodes — compete (PoW) or are selected (PoS) to produce new blocks; earn block rewards and transaction fees
Archive Nodes — store the complete historical state of the blockchain including all intermediate states; needed for blockchain explorers and analytics
Bootstrap Nodes — help new nodes discover peers when first joining the network (DNS seeds in Bitcoin)

slides.title: Cryptographic Hashing
slides.subtitle: The Mathematical Backbone of Blockchain Security
slides.description: A cryptographic hash function takes any input of any size and produces a fixed-length output (digest). The same input always gives the same output, but the output reveals nothing about the input. Bitcoin uses SHA-256 (256-bit output). Ethereum uses Keccak-256.

properties.desc: SHA-256('Hello') always returns the exact same 64-character hex string, on any computer, anywhere in the world
Given a hash output, it is computationally infeasible to find the original input. This is why passwords and private keys are safe as hashes
Changing even 1 bit of input flips approximately 50% of output bits. 'Hello' vs 'hello' produce completely different hashes
Finding two different inputs that produce the same hash output is computationally infeasible — probability is 1 in 2^256 for SHA-256

slides.example: SHA-256('Blockchain') = ef7797e13d3a75526946a3bcf00daec9fc9d1a6aa4083d7ebb11a9b33b6e6a41 | Ethereum uses Keccak-256 for address derivation and transaction signing

slides.title: Public Key Cryptography & Digital Signatures
leftItems: Every account has a key pair: Private Key (secret) + Public Key (shareable)
Private Key: 256-bit random number — never share this, it controls your funds
Public Key: derived from private key using Elliptic Curve Multiplication (secp256k1 curve)
Ethereum Address: last 20 bytes of Keccak-256 hash of the public key
Key relationship is one-way: public key cannot be used to derive private key
HD Wallets (BIP-32): one seed phrase (12/24 words) generates a tree of key pairs
rightItems: Step 1: User creates a transaction (to, value, data, nonce, gas)
Step 2: Transaction is hashed using Keccak-256
Step 3: Private key signs the hash using ECDSA algorithm — produces (r, s, v) signature
Step 4: Anyone can use the signature + transaction data to recover the signer's public key
Step 5: Network verifies signature without ever seeing the private key
Nonce: a counter preventing replay attacks — each transaction from an address increments by 1

slides.title: Consensus Mechanisms
leftItems: Miners race to find a nonce such that SHA-256(block header) < difficulty target
Difficulty auto-adjusts every 2016 blocks (~2 weeks) in Bitcoin to maintain 10-min block time
Finding the nonce requires trillions of hash attempts — pure brute force
Verifying a valid block takes one hash computation — asymmetric by design
51% attack: to rewrite history, attacker needs more than half the network's hash power
Energy: Bitcoin PoW consumes ~120 TWh/year — comparable to a mid-sized country
Used by: Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Dogecoin
rightItems: Validators lock up (stake) cryptocurrency as collateral to participate in block production
Block proposer is selected pseudo-randomly, weighted by stake size
Slashing: dishonest validators lose a portion of their staked funds as penalty
Ethereum requires 32 ETH (~$100K+) to run a validator node
Finality: Ethereum's Casper achieves economic finality — reverting a finalized block would cost attacker 1/3 of total staked ETH
Energy: Ethereum's switch to PoS (The Merge, Sep 2022) cut energy use by ~99.95%
Other PoS variants: DPoS (EOS), NPoS (Polkadot), LPoS (Tezos)

properties.title: Immutability
properties.desc: Confirmed blocks are cryptographically sealed. Altering past data requires redoing all subsequent proof-of-work — economically infeasible on established networks

properties.title: Transparency
properties.desc: Every transaction is permanently public and auditable by anyone with a blockchain explorer. There is no hidden activity on a public chain

properties.title: Decentralization
properties.desc: Thousands of independent nodes worldwide maintain identical copies. No single company, government, or person controls the network

properties.title: Trustlessness
properties.desc: Parties interact via cryptographic proofs and protocol rules, not promises or legal agreements. Code enforces the contract

properties.title: Programmability
properties.desc: Smart contracts are programs stored on-chain that execute automatically when triggered. They enable DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, and more

properties.title: Censorship Resistance
properties.desc: No authority can block a valid transaction. Anyone with the correct private key can broadcast to the network and expect inclusion

slides.title: Ethereum & the EVM
slides.definition: Ethereum is a programmable blockchain — a 'world computer' where anyone can deploy and run decentralized applications (dApps). The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is the sandboxed runtime environment that executes smart contract bytecode on every node in the network.
keyPoints: Proposed by Vitalik Buterin in 2013; launched in July 2015 — extended Bitcoin's idea with a Turing-complete scripting language
EVM: a stack-based virtual machine with 256-bit word size; executes bytecode compiled from Solidity, Vyper, or other EVM-compatible languages
Gas: every EVM operation (opcode) costs a fixed amount of gas; users pay gas fees in ETH to compensate validators for computation
Gas Limit: the maximum gas a transaction is willing to use; prevents infinite loops from halting the network (the Halting Problem solution)
EIP-1559 (London Upgrade, 2021): introduced base fee (burned) + priority tip (to validator); made gas fees more predictable
EVM Compatibility: Polygon, BNB Chain, Avalanche C-Chain, Arbitrum, Optimism all run the EVM — Solidity contracts deploy across all these chains with minimal changes
State: Ethereum is a state machine — every block transitions the global state (all account balances + contract storage) from one valid state to another

slides.title: Smart Contracts — What & Why
leftItems: A program deployed to the blockchain at a fixed address — immutable once deployed
Written in Solidity (or Vyper), compiled to EVM bytecode, stored on-chain
Executes automatically when called — no human or server needed to run it
Has its own ETH balance and persistent storage (key-value store)
Anyone can read its code (open source by default on Etherscan)
Interactions are transactions — each call is recorded on-chain permanently
Cannot be stopped, modified, or censored once deployed (unless coded with an upgrade mechanism)
rightItems: DeFi — Uniswap (DEX), Aave (lending), MakerDAO (stablecoin DAI) — billions in TVL
NFTs — ERC-721 contracts store ownership of digital assets; OpenSea, Blur
DAOs — Decentralized Autonomous Organizations vote via token governance (Compound, Uniswap DAO)
Stablecoins — USDC, USDT, DAI are ERC-20 contracts that manage token supply
Bridges — cross-chain token transfers via lock-and-mint smart contract pairs
Gaming — in-game assets as NFTs; play-to-earn mechanics (Axie Infinity, Gods Unchained)
Identity — on-chain credentials, verifiable attestations (ENS — Ethereum Name Service)

slides.title: Solidity — Introduction to the Language
slides.definition: Solidity is a statically-typed, compiled, object-oriented programming language designed specifically for writing smart contracts on the EVM. Its syntax is heavily influenced by JavaScript, C++, and Python. Solidity files use the .sol extension.
keyPoints: Current stable version: Solidity 0.8.x — introduced built-in overflow/underflow protection (pre-0.8 required SafeMath library)
SPDX License Identifier: every file should start with // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT (or GPL-3.0, UNLICENSED, etc.)
pragma solidity ^0.8.0; — declares the compiler version; ^ means 'compatible with 0.8.x but not 0.9.x'
Compiled by solc (Solidity Compiler) into: ABI (Application Binary Interface) + Bytecode. ABI defines how to call the contract. Bytecode is what gets deployed
Development tools: Remix IDE (browser-based, perfect for beginners), Hardhat (Node.js framework), Foundry (Rust-based, fast testing)
Every deployed contract has a unique address — interactions happen by sending transactions to that address with encoded function call data

slides.title: Solidity — Data Types & State Variables
leftItems: bool — true / false (1 byte storage)
uint256 — unsigned integer 0 to 2^256-1 (most common); also uint8, uint16...uint128
int256 — signed integer -2^255 to 2^255-1; also int8...int128
address — 20-byte Ethereum address; address payable can receive ETH
bytes32 — fixed-size 32-byte array; cheapest way to store short strings on-chain
bytes1 to bytes32 — fixed-size byte arrays
enum — user-defined type with named constants; stored as uint8
rightItems: string — dynamic UTF-8 string; expensive to store on-chain
bytes — dynamic byte array; more gas-efficient than string for raw data
array[] — dynamic or fixed-size arrays of any type
mapping(key => value) — hash table; keys are hashed, values stored at that slot
struct — groups multiple variables under one named type
Storage: persists between calls — most expensive (SSTORE opcode = 20,000 gas for new slot)
Memory: temporary within a function call — cheap; erased after execution
Calldata: read-only, non-modifiable — used for external function arguments; cheapest

slides.title: Solidity — Functions & Visibility
leftItems: public — callable from anywhere: inside contract, derived contracts, and externally
private — only callable within the same contract; not inherited
internal — callable within the contract AND derived (child) contracts; not externally
external — only callable from outside the contract; more gas-efficient for large arguments (uses calldata)
Getter functions for public state variables are auto-generated by the compiler
Constructor — special function that runs ONCE at deployment; sets initial state
rightItems: view — reads state but does NOT modify it; free to call (no gas if called externally)
pure — neither reads nor modifies state; mathematical/utility functions
payable — allows function to receive ETH; required to accept Ether transfers
returns(type) — declares return type; use named returns for clarity
modifier — reusable code that runs before/after a function (e.g., onlyOwner, nonReentrant)
virtual — marks function as overridable in derived contracts
override — indicates function overrides a parent virtual function

slides.title: Solidity — Mappings, Arrays & Structs
leftItems: mapping(address => uint256) public balances — maps each address to a token balance
Values default to zero for unmapped keys — no KeyError like Python
Cannot iterate over a mapping — you must track keys manually with an array
Nested mappings: mapping(address => mapping(address => uint256)) allowances — used in ERC-20 token approvals
Mappings can only exist in storage — cannot be used in memory or as function parameters
Gas cost: reading a mapping slot = 2,100 gas (cold) or 100 gas (warm, EIP-2929)
rightItems: uint256[] public numbers — dynamic array; .push(), .pop(), .length
uint256[10] public fixed — fixed array; size cannot change after declaration
Deleting from middle of array leaves a gap (gas-efficient trick: swap with last, then pop)
struct Student { string name; uint256 grade; bool enrolled; } — groups related data
Structs can be stored in mappings: mapping(uint256 => Student) public students
Packing: declaring uint128 a; uint128 b; in a struct packs them into one 32-byte storage slot — saves gas vs two uint256

slides.title: Solidity — Events & Error Handling
leftItems: Events emit logs stored on the blockchain — cheaper than storage (375 gas base)
event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value)
emit Transfer(msg.sender, recipient, amount) — triggers the event
Indexed parameters (up to 3) are stored in bloom filters — efficiently searchable by dApps
Frontend apps (ethers.js / web3.js) listen for events to update UI in real-time
Events are NOT accessible from within Solidity — they are only for off-chain consumption
Standard: ERC-20 requires Transfer and Approval events for all token movements
rightItems: require(condition, 'error message') — reverts with message if condition false; use for input validation and access control
revert('reason') — unconditionally reverts; use inside if-else for complex conditions
assert(condition) — reverts with Panic error if false; use only for internal invariants that should never fail
custom error MyError(address caller) — Solidity 0.8.4+; more gas-efficient than string messages
revert MyError(msg.sender) — uses custom error; saves ~50% gas vs require with string
try/catch — handles errors from external contract calls and contract creation
All reverts are atomic — all state changes in the call are undone; gas used is NOT refunded

slides.title: Solidity — Inheritance & Interfaces
leftItems: contract MyToken is ERC20 — inherits all state and functions of ERC20
Multiple inheritance: contract C is A, B — resolved using C3 linearization (same as Python MRO)
super.functionName() — explicitly calls the parent implementation
abstract contract — has at least one unimplemented function; cannot be deployed directly
OpenZeppelin Contracts library provides battle-tested base contracts: ERC20, ERC721, Ownable, AccessControl, ReentrancyGuard
Import: import '@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol' — npm or Hardhat dependency
rightItems: interface IERC20 — declares function signatures only; no implementation, no state variables
Used to interact with external contracts whose source code you may not have
IERC20(tokenAddress).transfer(to, amount) — calls transfer on any ERC-20 token
library SafeMath — stateless, reusable code; called with delegatecall; no storage of its own
using SafeMath for uint256 — attaches library functions to a type (pre-0.8 pattern)
Post-Solidity 0.8: built-in overflow protection makes SafeMath obsolete
Interfaces + events define the ABI — the standard that dApps use to communicate with contracts

slides.title: DeFi, NFTs & The Ethereum Ecosystem
slides.intro: The programmability of Ethereum has spawned a multi-trillion dollar ecosystem of decentralized applications. As developers, understanding these protocols is essential — you may be building the next one.
bullets: ERC-20 (Fungible Tokens) — the standard for cryptocurrencies and governance tokens; defines transfer, approve, allowance, balanceOf, totalSupply functions
ERC-721 (NFTs) — Non-Fungible Tokens; each token has a unique tokenId; used for digital art, game items, real estate deeds — OpenSea, Blur
ERC-1155 (Multi-Token) — single contract manages both fungible and non-fungible tokens; used in blockchain gaming for efficiency
DeFi Primitives — DEXes (Uniswap AMM model), Lending (Aave overcollateralized loans), Yield Farming, Liquid Staking (Lido stETH)
Layer 2 Scaling — Arbitrum & Optimism (Optimistic Rollups), zkSync & StarkNet (ZK Rollups) — execute transactions off-chain, post proofs to Ethereum L1; 10-100x cheaper gas
DAOs — Compound, Uniswap, ENS governed entirely by token holders via on-chain proposals and voting; no CEO or board of directors

slides.title: Development Tools & Workflow
leftItems: Remix IDE — browser-based; no installation; perfect for learning and quick prototyping; built-in compiler, deployer, and debugger
Hardhat — Node.js development framework; scripting in JavaScript/TypeScript; local Ethereum network (hardhat node); industry standard
Foundry — Rust-based toolchain (forge, cast, anvil); tests written in Solidity; extremely fast; growing rapidly in professional teams
OpenZeppelin Contracts — audited, production-ready base contracts; install via npm; essential for secure token and access control development
ethers.js / viem — JavaScript libraries for frontend interaction with deployed contracts; read state, send transactions, listen to events
rightItems: Unit Tests — test each function in isolation; Hardhat uses Mocha + Chai; Foundry uses Solidity assertions
Local Network — hardhat node or anvil; fork mainnet for integration testing with real protocols
Testnets — Sepolia (Ethereum), Mumbai (Polygon); get free test ETH from faucets; deploy and test before mainnet
Mainnet Deployment — use Hardhat Ignition or Foundry scripts; verify source code on Etherscan (--verify flag)
Gas Optimization — use mappings over arrays for lookups; pack structs; use calldata not memory; emit events instead of storage where possible
Security Audits — always audit before mainnet for high-value contracts; common tools: Slither (static analysis), Echidna (fuzzing)

slides.title: Summary & Your Learning Path
points: Blockchain = distributed, cryptographically-linked, tamper-proof ledger maintained by consensus across a decentralized peer-to-peer network
Cryptographic hashing (SHA-256 / Keccak-256) and digital signatures (ECDSA) underpin all blockchain security — no trusted third party needed
Consensus mechanisms (PoW, PoS) solve the Byzantine Generals Problem — achieving agreement among untrusted, distributed participants
Ethereum extends blockchain with the EVM — a programmable world computer where smart contracts execute automatically and trustlessly
Solidity is your primary tool: master data types, functions, mappings, events, inheritance, and security patterns to build on the EVM
The ecosystem is vast: ERC-20, ERC-721, DeFi, DAOs, Layer 2 — all built from the smart contract primitives you are learning in this course
Next steps: Build a complete ERC-20 token, deploy to Sepolia testnet, write unit tests in Hardhat, and explore one DeFi protocol's source code
slides.closing: The code you write in Solidity becomes unstoppable, globally-accessible financial infrastructure. Build responsibly.
